intro: These are our own tests of what Qloo adds, written before they ran and reported whichever way they came out. The short version: Qloo is not a better recommender than a strong language model, and we do not claim it is. It is good at a few specific things, and the product is built on those.

proofs.title: Does Qloo predict what people will love, from what they already picked?
proofs.method: Hid 30% of each person's picks from public listening and film data and asked each method to predict them: Qloo's graph, an AI alone, and plain popularity.
proofs.result: Music, recall at 20: Qloo 0.157, popularity 0.061, an AI alone 0.186. Films: Qloo 0.050, popularity 0.083, an AI alone 0.066.
proofs.verdict_text: Beats popularity on music; does not beat an AI alone; loses on films.
proofs.limits: Public data from real people, but not our own guests. It changed the design: Qloo is not used as a recommender of last resort.

proofs.title: Places: a fixed Qloo-then-AI pipeline against an AI alone
proofs.method: Thirty New York questions; recommendations scored against what locals picked.
proofs.result: In the requested area: 99.7% against 93.5%. Closed or not found: 1.3% against 7.3%. Agreeing with locals, precision at 10: 0.047 against 0.127.
proofs.verdict_text: Stays in the area and avoids dead listings; worse at agreeing with locals.
proofs.limits: Closure could not be measured independently, so the closure figure is not firm.

proofs.title: Do Qloo's place filters do what they say?
proofs.method: Radius, price and rating filters checked against what came back.
proofs.result: All 239 results were inside the radius. Usable results 63.2% against 37.0% at the floor, and 89.5% against 81.7% at the ceiling.

proofs.title: Are crowd groups stable enough to show an owner?
proofs.method: Soft groups from listening tags, refitted on resampled crowds, compared with shuffled versions of the same crowd.
proofs.result: Stability rises with crowd size; groups are shown from 60 guests (provisional) and named from 200. Our product code reproduces the research figures within 0.004 on the same data.
proofs.verdict_text: Groups exist and repeat, at the sizes we say.
proofs.limits: Stability, not usefulness: we have not shown that owners act on the groups. Real five-pick survey data is untested.

proofs.title: The fixed pipeline again, on New York places
proofs.method: Qloo bounds the candidates, an AI picks and explains.
proofs.result: Precision at 10: 0.073 against 0.127 for an AI alone. Qloo's candidate pool held about 15% of what locals picked.
proofs.verdict_text: A fixed pipeline did not beat an AI alone, so we dropped it.
proofs.limits: This result is why Nigiwai is not built that way.

proofs.title: A tool-using agent that runs Qloo calls itself and lists only venues Qloo returned
proofs.method: Same thirty questions, preregistered; forty music users for the music test.
proofs.result: Places: precision at 10 0.180 against 0.127, recall 0.250 against 0.168, every venue in the requested area. Music: tied the AI alone (recall at 20 within 0.002) and clearly beat popularity.
proofs.verdict_text: Beat an AI alone on places; tied on music.
proofs.limits: Part of the gain is the multi-step, verify-before-listing design, not Qloo itself (see H). Single runs, same model family wrote the baseline.

proofs.title: Are groups stable on Qloo's own tags?
proofs.method: 319 people, 767 Qloo calls, groups refitted on resampled crowds.
proofs.result: Raw stability 0.649 at 200 people, 0.569 at 100 and 0.508 at 60: about the same as on listening tags.
proofs.verdict_text: Qloo tags give stable groups, no better than a free tag source.

proofs.title: Is Qloo what makes the agent good at places?
proofs.method: The same agent and rules with a free OpenStreetMap tool instead of Qloo, same thirty questions.
proofs.result: Precision at 10 0.167 against 0.180; recall 0.237 against 0.250. The differences were not distinguishable (the test could only detect gaps of about 0.06 to 0.09).
proofs.verdict_text: On New York places, Qloo's own contribution to accuracy is not shown.
proofs.limits: Absence of evidence, not proof of equivalence. We do not claim that Qloo drives place accuracy.

proofs.title: Taste across categories: from music picks to book picks
proofs.method: Thirty-three Reddit threads: picks in one category, predict picks in another.
proofs.result: Precision at 10: the Qloo agent 0.038, an AI alone 0.107, a free-data agent 0.095.
proofs.verdict_text: Clearly worse than an AI alone.
proofs.limits: One kind of question. It is why Soundcheck uses artists as seeds for artists and never crosses categories.

proofs.title: Hybrids: can Qloo improve an AI's list?
proofs.method: Thirty-one fresh threads. Qloo as a re-ranker, as a filter, as a tag source.
proofs.result: As a re-ranker, clearly worse than an AI alone (precision at 10 0.106 against 0.169); as a filter or tag source, no better. Qloo's affinity ranked the consensus items at chance (AUC 0.508).
proofs.verdict_text: Qloo did not improve an AI's list.
proofs.limits: On this task. Taste fit beyond famous items, cold start and real-user judgement are untested.

proofs.title: Who is in a crowd: age and gender from Qloo's audience data
proofs.method: Entities with common-knowledge audiences, directions fixed in advance; fresh entities in the second run.
proofs.result: Gender direction right for 27 of 27. Younger against older separated at AUC 0.96 to 0.97 on a contrast measure. Three-item crowds told apart 400 of 400 times (from only 35 and 10 distinct triples).
proofs.verdict_text: A coarse age and gender reading is directionally right.
proofs.limits: Ground truth is common knowledge, not a survey; accuracy is not verified. Shown as modelled.

proofs.title: Does an act score highest for the crowd it belongs to?
proofs.method: Twenty acts scored against three seed crowds (pop, crooners, hard rock).
proofs.result: The highest-scoring crowd was the expected one 20 of 20 times. In the product, on a real run: 6 of 6 acts fit their own crowd best.
proofs.verdict_text: Works on distant crowds; an AI alone would likely match it on famous names.
proofs.limits: Easy, genre-separated cases. Close cases and non-artist ideas are untested, and the score weights are not calibrated against outcomes.

proofs.title: Does an audience filter change which places Qloo returns?
proofs.method: Age and gender filters on place searches in five cities.
proofs.result: No. All seven audience conditions returned the same twenty places in the same order, in all five cities.
proofs.verdict_text: The filter has no effect, so the product does not offer it.
proofs.limits: With no interest seed or audience id; those are untested.

proofs.title: Obscure artists: does Qloo know what an AI does not?
proofs.method: Twenty-seven obscure artists; does each tool know the act exists?
proofs.result: Existence: Qloo 0.895, an AI alone 0.800, not significantly different. The AI said it did not know 4 of 27.
proofs.verdict_text: Not distinguishable on existence; relevance was not measured.
proofs.limits: This is why the product shows both answers side by side and marks which acts are real Qloo entities, instead of claiming a win.

proofs.title: Can public event lineups start a venue's crowd?
proofs.method: Performers from MusicBrainz event records at three real venues, matched to Qloo by exact name.
proofs.result: 56% of sampled performers resolved exactly to a Qloo artist (69% at Mercury Lounge).
proofs.verdict_text: Enough to start from, never fuzzy-matched.
proofs.limits: Smaller rooms book local acts Qloo does not know, so the view is partial; a near miss is usually a different artist, so none is accepted.

build.title: Taste Card call budget
build.result: Two hundred synthetic scans through the real survey and card endpoints, live Qloo: a mean of 1.75 Qloo calls per card (maximum 3); the instant card answered in under 1.5 s every time; the fill-in took a median of 3.5 s.

build.title: Audience reading in the product, live
build.result: Three real crowds went through the survey, the groups job and the audience step: younger-leaning and women, older-leaning and no clear lean, older-leaning and men: as common knowledge says. Three live calls.

build.title: Soundcheck in the product, live
build.result: Three crowds of well-known artists, six acts with known audiences: each act fit its own crowd's group best (6 of 6, after fixing an act that was one of the crowd's own favourites).

reading: What Qloo is measurably good for here: staying inside the area and honouring filters, exact entity identifiers so nothing is invented, and a taste graph that covers obscure acts. It is not shown to recommend better than a strong language model. That is why every Soundcheck shows an AI's answer beside Qloo's, and why the numbers that matter come from your own guests.
